title: Signature What AI Disclosure Means
body:
The Signature Open Hand is an original Signature design in which every machine-assisted work carries an open hand: a visible mark stating what the machine did, placed where the audience meets the work. The hand is open, not hidden behind a menu, and it names the role in plain words, such as drafted, illustrated, voiced, or edited. A work without its hand is treated as unfinished, however polished it looks.

Method. To show the hand, name the machine's role at the work's first meeting with its audience, keep the hand with every copy and excerpt, and update the hand when the machine's role changes in a revision. If the machine's role was trivial, such as correcting spelling, the hand may say so briefly, so audiences learn to distinguish small assistance from substantial generation.

Checklist.

  • Mark placed at first meeting with audience
  • Role named in plain words
  • Hand travels with copies and excerpts
  • Hand updated on revision
  • Trivial assistance named briefly

title: Signature Visible Labels: Where a Label Belongs
body:
The Signature First Frame is an original Signature design that puts the disclosure in the first frame of every machine-assisted work: the first image corner, the first seconds of video, the first line of audio notes, the first line beneath a byline. A work whose first frame carries its hand cannot be mistaken at first glance, and a work that is cropped or clipped still carries the hand in its opening, where cropping rarely reaches.

Method. To frame a work, place the hand in the first frame before any other credit or decoration, keep it in the same visual language as the work so it is not dismissed as a watermark to be cropped, and repeat it in the description. If a format forces cropping, place a second hand deeper in the work, so at least one hand survives ordinary editing.

Checklist.

  • Hand in the first frame
  • Before other credits or decoration
  • Repeated in the description
  • Second hand deeper in cropped formats
  • Hand in the work's own visual language

title: Signature Disclosure Wording Audiences Understand
body:
The Signature Plain Sentence is an original Signature design that limits every disclosure to one sentence of plain words, built from a fixed pattern: this work was, the machine's action, and the person's action. The pattern prevents both jargon and evasion, since a disclosure that cannot be written in the pattern must be rewritten until it can. A creator who uses the pattern everywhere gives their audience a single recognisable promise.

Method. To write the sentence, fill the pattern with the true machine action and the true human action, using ordinary verbs, and place the sentence where the audience meets the work. If the human action was only a glance, say reviewed briefly rather than claiming a full check, and if there was no human check, say so, since an honest absence is more trustworthy than an invented check.

Checklist.

  • Pattern: work, machine action, person action
  • Ordinary verbs only
  • Human check described truthfully
  • No check means saying so
  • Same pattern across all work

title: Signature Provenance Metadata: What Travels With a File
body:
The Signature Travelling Record is an original Signature design that attaches a plain-language history to every machine-assisted file: made by, made with, edited by, and published by, each in one line. The record travels inside the file's description wherever the file goes, and any copy that loses the record is treated as undisclosed until the record is restored. The design values a readable history over a technical one, since audiences act on what they can read.

Method. To keep the travelling record, write the four lines at creation, add a line for each significant edit, and copy the record with the file on every export and upload. If an export strips the record, restore it in the description before sharing, and never publish a file whose record is missing without adding a visible label explaining the gap.

Checklist.

  • Four lines: made by, made with, edited by, published by
  • Line added per significant edit
  • Record copied on every export
  • Stripped record restored before sharing
  • Gap explained with a visible label

title: Signature Watermarking: Visible, Invisible, and Their Limits
body:
The Signature Double Mark is an original Signature design that pairs every machine-assisted work with two marks that serve different readers: a visible hand for the audience and a travelling note for tools and later checkers. The visible hand is never removed for presentation, and the travelling note is restored whenever an export loses it. A work that loses one mark is repaired before sharing, so the pair is treated as part of the work rather than as decoration.

Method. To apply the double mark, place the visible hand at the work's first meeting with its audience, attach the travelling note to the file's description, and check both marks after every export, crop, or upload. If either mark is lost, restore it before sharing, and if restoration is impossible, add a plain statement of the machine's role in the work's place.

Checklist.

  • Visible hand for the audience
  • Travelling note for checkers
  • Both checked after every export
  • Lost mark restored before sharing
  • Impossible restoration replaced by a statement

title: Signature Disclosing Degrees: Help, Editing, and Generation
body:
The Signature Degree Scale is an original Signature design with three named degrees: hand, loom, and mill. Hand means the machine assisted small parts, loom means the machine wove substantial content a person then edited, and mill means the machine produced the work wholesale from a prompt. The scale's names are deliberately plain, so an audience that has never heard of a model can still tell a hand work from a mill work at a glance.

Method. To use the scale, grade each work by its largest machine role, mark the grade beside the work's hand, and describe the human check that followed in the same place. Use the scale consistently across all work, never grading the same kind of production differently in different places, and revisit the grade when a revision changes the machine's role.

Checklist.

  • Hand: small assistance
  • Loom: substantial machine content, human-edited
  • Mill: wholesale machine production
  • Grade by largest machine role
  • Grade revisited when role changes

title: Signature Disclosure by Medium: Image, Audio, Video, Text
body:

The hand's shape changes with the medium, but its meaning never does, so an audience that learns one hand can recognise the others. title: Signature Disclosure in News, Research, and Education
body:
The Signature Trust Ledger is an original Signature design for trust-sensitive work: a ledger entry per published piece, recording the machine's role, the human check, the sources checked, and the corrections made. The ledger is kept beside the work and summarised in the disclosure, so an audience that doubts a piece can see its verification trail without asking the author for private notes. A piece without a ledger entry is not published in trust-sensitive contexts.

Method. To keep the ledger, record the machine's role and the human check at publication, list the sources a person checked for factual claims, and add corrections as new entries rather than silently editing old ones. Summarise the ledger in the disclosure in plain words, keep the full ledger available to the institution, and review ledger practice when an error escapes, since an escaped error shows a gap in the ledger, not just in the piece.

Checklist.

  • Entry per published piece
  • Machine role and human check recorded
  • Sources checked listed
  • Corrections added as new entries

title: Signature When Disclosure Is Required: Checking the Rules
body:
The Signature Rule Map is an original Signature design that maps every publication against its layers before release: platform, publisher, contract, and law, each with its own box to tick and its own note of what was found. A work is not released until every box carries either a tick or a note explaining why the layer does not apply, so no layer is silently skipped. The map is kept with the work's record, so a later republication starts from the last map rather than from memory.

Method. To draw the map, list the four layers for the work's first publication place, check each in turn, and record the finding in its box. On republication, redraw the map for the new place, since layers change with place, and keep old maps beside new ones so the work's disclosure history stays readable. Where a layer is unclear, the map records the uncertainty and the choice to disclose more, rather than hiding the doubt.

Checklist.

  • Four layers listed per publication
  • Each box ticked or explained
  • No silent skipping
  • Map redrawn on republication
  • Uncertainty recorded, disclosure widened

title: Signature Correcting a Missing Disclosure
body:
The Signature Late Hand is an original Signature design for corrections: a hand added after publication carries a date and a brief note that it was late, so the audience can see both the disclosure and its history. The late hand is placed with the same prominence as an on-time hand, and the work's record notes why it was late, so the same workflow gap does not lose the next hand. A late hand honestly dated is treated as a repair, not as a failure to hide.

Method. To add a late hand, place the disclosure where the audience meets the work, add the date and a brief note of lateness, and correct controlled copies with the same hand. Publish the correction with similar prominence where the work travelled widely, record the workflow gap that caused the lateness, and fix that gap before the next publication.

Checklist.

  • Hand dated and noted as late
  • Same prominence as on-time hand
  • Controlled copies corrected
  • Workflow gap recorded
  • Gap fixed before next publication

title: Signature AI-Edited Versus AI-Generated Work
body:
The Signature Substance Test is an original Signature design that grades a work by substance rather than by touch: the grader asks who supplied the ideas, the structure, and the expression, and grades by the largest share. A work whose ideas and structure came from a person but whose sentences were polished by a machine is a hand work; a work whose sentences came from a machine is a loom or mill work even if a person edited every line afterwards. The test is written on the work's record, so the grade can be checked.

Method. To apply the test, list the work's ideas, structure, and expression, name the supplier of each, and grade by the largest machine share. Record the test beside the disclosure, so an audience that questions the grade can see the reasoning, and regrade when a revision changes the shares, since a work that grows more machine-made in revision must not keep an earlier human grade.

Checklist.

  • Ideas, structure, expression listed
  • Supplier named for each
  • Grade by largest machine share
  • Test recorded beside disclosure
  • Regrade when shares change

title: Signature Audience Trust: What Hidden Disclosure Costs
body:
The Signature Trust Account is an original Signature design that treats disclosure as an account: every honest disclosure deposits trust, every hidden role withdraws it, and every prompt correction repays part of a withdrawal. The account is not a score shown to audiences, but a discipline for creators: a creator who watches their own account will disclose before publication, because depositing on time is cheaper than repaying after discovery. The account's balance is judged by the creator's own consistency, not by any public ranking.

Method. To keep the account, disclose at publication as a matter of routine, correct discoveries promptly and publicly, and review the account when planning new work, asking whether the planned disclosure matches the planned machine role. If the account shows a pattern of late disclosures, fix the workflow that causes lateness before publishing more work, since a pattern of lateness is itself a disclosure about the creator's practice.

Checklist.

  • Disclose at publication routinely
  • Correct discoveries promptly
  • Review account before new work
  • Late pattern means fix the workflow
  • Balance judged by consistency

title: Signature Disclosure in Advertising and Sponsored Content
body:
The Signature Twin Label is an original Signature design for sponsored machine-assisted content: two labels side by side, one for sponsorship and one for the machine's role, in the same size and the same place. The twin design prevents either label from hiding behind the other, since an audience that sees one label sees both, and a creator who removes one label visibly breaks the pair. The pair is kept together through excerpts and reshares as a single unit.

Method. To apply the twin label, write both labels in plain words, place them side by side at the content's first meeting with its audience, and treat them as one unit through editing and sharing: if one travels, both travel. If a format cannot carry both, choose a format that can, or do not publish the sponsored machine-made content in that format, since a format that forces a missing label is the wrong format for the work.

Checklist.

  • Two labels side by side, same size
  • Sponsorship and machine role both plain
  • Pair treated as one unit
  • Both travel with excerpts

title: Signature AI Voices and Likenesses: Consent and Disclosure
body:
The Signature Likeness Seal is an original Signature design for synthetic people: a seal that states synthesis, likeness source, and consent in three lines beside any synthetic voice or face. An original character carries a seal saying so, so audiences do not mistake it for a real person, and a real person's likeness carries a seal stating agreement, so audiences can trust the endorsement or performance. A synthetic person without a seal is not published, however convincing the synthesis.

Method. title: Signature Keeping Disclosure Records
body:
The Signature Version Scroll is an original Signature design that keeps a work's disclosure history as a scroll: each publication and revision adds a dated line, and no line is ever erased, so the work's making history can be read from first line to last. The scroll is summarised in the work's current disclosure, so audiences see the present truth, while the full scroll remains available to anyone who questions it. A work whose scroll is broken is treated as a work whose history is unknown, and disclosed as such.

Method. To keep the scroll, add a dated line at publication and at each revision, naming the machine's role and the disclosure's wording and placement for that version. Never erase a line; correct it with a new line that names the correction. Summarise the latest line in the current disclosure, and keep the scroll where the work's record lives, so it can be produced when a question arises.

Checklist.

  • Dated line per publication and revision
  • No line ever erased
  • Corrections added as new lines
  • Latest line summarised in disclosure
  • Scroll kept with the work's record

title: Signature A Disclosure Checklist for Every Publication
body:
The Signature Departure Check is an original Signature design that treats publication as a departure: a work does not leave the creator's hands until its departure check is complete, with every item ticked or marked not applicable with a reason. The check is printed on the work's record and signed by the creator, so a later question about disclosure can be answered by producing the check rather than by reconstructing memory. A work that fails its check waits, however eager its creator is to publish it.

Method. To run the departure check, work through the items in order, tick only items actually done, mark non-applicable items with a reason, and sign the check with the publication date. File the check with the version scroll, so the work's departure record and its history live together, and review failed checks as workflow lessons, fixing the step that most often fails before it fails another work.

Checklist.

  • Items worked in order
  • Tick only items actually done
  • Non-applicable items marked with reason
  • Check signed with publication date
  • Failed checks reviewed as lessons
